title: How God hides his face and the dragon is led
english: … or who give the body over to the stadium of martyrdom, or to the labours of the ascetic life, and in this way seem to destroy and kill themselves by being deprived of the enjoyments of life: “He who loses his life for my sake will find it” (Matthew 10:39). For one who perishes in this way, according to the Saviour's word, and finds his life, the prayer and the blessing is a great thing. Anyone of sound mind would pray that it might come upon him, and would wisely say: “The blessing,” and so on (Job 29:13).

“I was an eye to the blind, and a foot to the lame” (Job 29:15). As to the mind, he opened blind understandings and helped those maimed in soul, and he himself became their eye. To those lamed in the steps of the soul he gave feet; by his word he became their foot and led both by the hand. The eye stands for guidance of the understanding, the foot for guidance of conduct.

“I was a father of the powerless” (Job 29:16). These words show the voice of one who helps the powerless, the weak. “And a cause that I did not know, I searched out” (Job 29:16). You see his protection: it did not stop at money, nor at food and clothing; I stood forward even to the point of danger in another man's fight.

“And I broke the molars of the unjust” (Job 29:17). See how hard the thing was: he says that he set the matter right even when it had already been seized. Truly Christ, when he came, crushed the molars of the opposing powers. “The Lord has broken the molars of the lions” (Psalm 58:6), and it is written in the prophet: “From the midst of their teeth I snatched the prey” (Job 29:17).

“And I said: My age will grow old like the stem of a palm” (Job 29:18). See after how long a time he says this: not boasting or thinking great things of himself, but compelled to speak of God's providence, of the things in which he enjoyed it and of where he stands now.

“But now the least have laughed at me; now they admonish me in their turn, whose fathers I set at nought” (Job 30:1). Not that he made a practice of contempt, but that he knew them clearly, as the prophet said: “Every evildoer is set at nought before him” (Psalm 15:4). For he counted such people as nothing.
“And the strength of their hands, what is it to me? Over them the full end has perished. In want and famine he is barren, those who yesterday fled from waterless distress and misery” (Job 30:2-3).

From Olympiodorus and Origen: I did not even ask them for any help, he says, that they should use such words against me on that account. They had long owed a penalty, being wicked, and in a way the punishment flew away from them. Or else: they longed for death because of their extreme poverty and did not obtain it, and not even their want brought them to their senses so as to become begetters of good; they remained barren, those who only yesterday, a little while ago, had escaped from the desert and their misfortunes. He seems to disparage them as low-born, from obscure villages and poor fathers. “Over them the full end has perished”: that is, they never brought anything good to completion.

“Those who go round the mallows on an echoing place, whose food was mallows” (Job 30:4). Mallow is a plant, they say, that quickly fills the one who eats it. “On an echoing place”: that is, on ravines and rocky ground, for such places ring and give back the voices of those who speak. Or he calls echoing the wooded place where the breath of the winds stirs the trees and makes a sound. So he says that these men roamed the woods and the ravines and the places where running waters sound and babble; in their great want they searched out plants and scraped the roots of trees for food, as some comfort in their hunger.
“Dishonoured and despised, in want of every good thing” (Job 30:4). It is another wickedness to be like this even in poverty.
“For would that I could lay hands on myself” (Job 30:24). You see that he says “if I could” not because of weakness but because he was forbidden.
“And I have stood in the assembly crying out” (Job 30:28). Because of the excess of his sufferings he is not ashamed even of the crowd of the gathering.

“I have become a brother of sirens and a companion of ostriches” (Job 30:29). I have fallen, he says, into the wildness of the birds; I have forgotten my own nature, and I am in no better state than they.

“For I have stood in a just balance, and the Lord knows my innocence, if my foot has turned aside from the way …” (Job 31:6-7). What exactness! No one could say that I misused my former wealth and goods for idleness and dissipation and so pay this penalty and have been changed, God having laid on me a fitting medicine. For to the one who loves laughter and play and is given to luxury he fittingly sets the opposite …

title: Job's hospitality, Elihu's speech, and the night watches
english: … condition he would bring about, handing him over to a mournful life of many laments. But the one who even before these things shunned revels and drove off people who joke and play the clown, what reason could there be for him to fall into a sullen and downcast life? Since I was already withered and austere, I did not fall into the vices that belong to that life.
“And if my maidservants often said, ‘Who would grant us to be filled with his flesh?’, for I was very kind” (Job 31:31). That is, to enjoy his life, because I was sweet to them.

“No stranger lodged outside, and my door was open to everyone who came” (Job 31:32). For he did not only care for them by taking them in, but also supplied them with provisions against the poverty that would follow.
“And Job ceased from words” (Job 31:40). Job fell silent, giving them room to speak; but he took note, called God as witness and called down curses on himself, because his friends had been silenced.

“For I will speak while you listen, until you have examined the words, and I will attend to you” (Job 32:11-12). Either he is saying this: even when you were refuting, you did not refute as you should have; or that afterwards you fell silent. That is how it bears on “For I will speak while you listen.”

“For how do you say, ‘I am righteous, and he has not heard me’?” (Job 33:12). What then happened? He did not think this. Elihu supposed it, but Job did not speak with any such mind, that he was more righteous than God; he meant that he had done these things, and yet he did not charge God with injustice. Elihu supposed this. But he rightly charged those others, who had betrayed God's side and denied it.

“I will speak, that I may rest, when I have opened my lips” (Job 32:20). One who has found an intelligent hearer and is full of words finds rest in speaking, as though emptying out and casting off the excess; and he says, “I will speak, that I may rest.”

“He who did not feel shame before the face of one held in honour, nor knows how to pay honour to the great” (Job 34:19). For even if you do not know, you still ought to yield much to him and to his glory, so as not to seek to learn everything.
“For he will no longer lay it upon a man” (Job 34:23). He seems to be saying this: now the good and the bad lie with us, but in the age to come no longer.

“For as for the one who says to the Mighty One, ‘I have received; I will not take a pledge; apart from myself I shall see; you show me’” (Job 34:31-32). Some have interpreted it thus: no one dares to say to one who is stronger, “You have taken what is mine unjustly, not by way of a pledge, as though it were owed to you, and you have taken it against my will; show that you have done this with good reason.” But if no one dares to say these things to a man of power, how, he says, can you be so bold as to say such things against God?

Symmachus rendered it thus: “Since I have taken up speech towards God, I will not hold back; unhindered, you make it plain to me.” His meaning is this: since I have taken up speech on God's behalf, says Elihu, I do not hold back, but go on with the argument unhindered. And if I do not speak well, you make it plain, that is, refute the argument.

But I think rather that the text should be understood thus: it is not that, because I have chosen to speak on God's behalf, you must for that reason simply agree with me as well, as though I were demanding payment of a debt. “Apart from myself I shall see; you show me” means: apart from my own argument I want to know whether you have anything to say in reply. I keep silence so that you may speak; take up the argument, if you can.

“Look up to heaven” (Job 35:5). No lover of the world looks up to heaven. Let us not love the world, nor the things in the world (1 John 2:15). If we love the things here, we do not look up to heaven.

“If you have sinned, what will you do?” (Job 35:6). That is, you will not wrong him; but neither will you benefit him if you are righteous. For since he was saying, “If I have sinned, what can I do?” (Job 7:20), “What shall I do?” he says, this is in order to say: Why? Does he care about your sinning because he is wronged? As though he suffered harm?

“He who appoints night watches” (Job 35:10). Do you want to see how God appoints night watches? This whole age is night; it is darkness. The light is kept for you: the light you see now, you see through a mirror (1 Corinthians 13:12). And: “In your light we shall see light” (Psalm 36:9); one day we are to see it. Is not the whole age, then, night? Since it is night, there are many enemies; many wild beasts prowl about. Since, then, the affairs in the darkness of this life are night, there is need of guards posted for this night, so that the guards, those set over the nights, may keep watch over those who are in the night, and may come and guard us from the robbers. Who, then, are the guards posted by God in the night watches? “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and will deliver them” (Psalm 34:7). These are the angels who in the night …

added_allusions.note: Possible: 'What shall I do?' he says may recall LXX 35:3 τί ποιήσω ἁμαρτών; KJV 35:3 ('What profit shall I have') differs, so not cited in the text.

title: The measures of the earth, the bounds of the sea, and Job's answer
english: … keep guard over us.

“Who fixed its measures, if you know? Or who is it that stretched a line over it?” (Job 38:5). The Greeks did want to say something about the measure of the earth: the diameter of the earth, they say, is twenty-five myriads of stades. But the passage seems to show that the measure of the earth is beyond everyone's grasp; only the Saviour knows it, who is also the Creator. He said “measures,” and not “measure,” to set before us the differences in the earth. What is the measure of this or that land: of the East, say, which bears the spices? What is the measure of the land that bears pepper, or the animals? For not everything grows everywhere. These measures, then, are with the Word of God. So the earth has not come to be of this size without reason, nor by chance; it seems to me that if even the slightest thing were added, it would be out of place, and if anything were taken away, by the same reasoning it would spoil the whole earth. This is what the measures and the line hint at.

“And who is it that laid a cornerstone upon it?” (Job 38:6). Who is it that laid a cornerstone upon it, so that it stands so firmly fixed, as though built upon the secure footing of a foundation? By the will of God, for in his hand are all the ends of the earth (Psalm 95:4). “A cornerstone”: this can also be understood of the only-begotten Son of God, made flesh for our sake, according to the word in the Psalms: “The stone which they rejected has become the head of the corner” (Psalm 118:22). For coming to earth by the good pleasure of the Father, he joined in himself the two peoples, the Jews and the Gentiles, just as, of course, the cornerstone binds both walls together.

“And I said to it, ‘Thus far you shall come, and you shall not pass beyond’” (Job 38:11). Symmachus: “Up to here let the swelling of your waves be set.” So securely does he hold it in, as if with bars; and so easily, as if by a set order. For “I said,” he says, and there is no answering back, when this comes about with no constraint driving it, and that although great force and strength are lashing the sea. This is why he did not let it be calm or gentle: so that it might proclaim God's strength, its nature fighting against the command and the command everywhere prevailing. If the water were gentle, many would have credited its good order to the nature of water. But as it is, troubled, lashed, driven back within, and unable to pass its bounds, by its very turmoil it proclaims the strength of God.

“And who prepared food for the raven?” (Job 38:41). For it is said not to rear its young. The grown birds, naturally, being large, find food for themselves; but who rears the young? Is it not the word of God? As the Gospel too says: “The birds of the heaven do not sow, nor do they reap, and your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matthew 6:26).

“Is it at your command that the eagle mounts up, and the vulture, having settled on its nest, lodges on a jutting rock and in a hidden place?” (Job 39:27-28). … If among the flesh-eaters there is some reasoning wisdom, present in each from the knowledge it has by nature, and directed to knowing, for one of them war, for others the dead, you see it in the vulture too, a single bird borne through the air.

“Why am I still judged, being admonished and reproving the Lord, when I hear such things, I who am nothing?” (Job 40:4). “Why am I still judged?” he says, by way of a preface; and from the start he gave up the first place. I am beaten in my case before you, he says; why do you press the suit further? For what answer can be given? And how should one look such a master in the face? I, he says, kept on seeking the cause of the blow that fell on me; but I brought no charge against the work of creation, and I have nothing to say against what has been said. Something is left unsaid: as one not even reproving the Lord, the wretched man being admonished.

“But gird your loins like a man; I will ask you, and you answer me” (Job 40:7). For those who are confident in an abundance of just claims do not even shun their opponents but give them leave, so that the victory may come out of that abundance. Then he also makes his defence to him: I care about human beings; it is plain from this why I brought this trial upon you. I give you freedom to speak: I will ask you, and you answer me.

“Do you think that I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be shown to be righteous?” (Job 40:8). He means the present divine answer: I do not say these things to condemn you, he says, but to show you righteous. Or he is speaking of the trial, calling the permission a divine dealing, that is: that I had ordained this to happen for some other reason. He did not say, “that you might become,” but, “that you might appear as what you were,” so that you might teach the others. And see: he did not say, “that you might become righteous” (for the righteousness which with exactness you …
